claims.text: Rapid SPS processing of a Mg-containing lightweight HEA produces an initially homogeneous single-phase microstructure.
The initial single phase is a metastable, supersaturated Mg-containing solid solution.
The SPS-processed initial alloy has a density below 6 g/cm3.
Post-sintering thermal treatment activates Mg diffusion and drives phase separation from the supersaturated matrix.
During thermal exposure, Mg preferentially segregates to grain boundaries.
Mg segregation produces Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates along grain boundaries and within the matrix.
Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates interrupt formation of a continuous protective oxide layer.
The disrupted oxide layer causes faster and less uniform high-temperature oxidation.
Mg-rich intermetallic regions become sites of localized electrochemical activity.
The localized electrochemical activity reduces corrosion resistance and increases corrosion current density.
The untreated as-sintered baseline has a well-integrated passivating film and relatively stable corrosion behavior.
The untreated as-sintered baseline oxidizes more slowly than the thermally aged material.
Thermally treated samples will have a greater volume fraction or area coverage of Mg-rich intermetallic phases than as-sintered controls.
Thermally treated samples will develop thicker or more rapidly growing and less uniform oxide scales than as-sintered controls.
The proposed mechanism applies only when exposure activates Mg diffusion without causing complete transformation to other equilibrium phases.
Interactions with other alloying elements may alter Mg segregation, oxide formation, and corrosion behavior under different thermal histories.
